L33: ## Can middle schoolers take college classes?
L34: 
L35: Yes. With no minimum age requirement, Universal Learner Courses give academically prepared middle school students access to college level coursework. For families exploring college courses for middle school students, this can be particularly valuable when a student has advanced beyond their current curriculum or developed a strong interest in a particular subject.
L36: Families should consider whether their student is prepared for independent learning, college-level assignments and managing coursework deadlines. Starting with one course can be a useful way to assess that readiness.
L37: 
L38: Odin Halvorsen enrolled in his first ASU course at 13 years old.
L39: 
L40: “The experience made me feel more independent as a student,” Halvorsen said. “It gave me a preview of what college courses will be like.”
L41: ## How to take college classes in high school
L42: 
L43: For homeschool high school students, Universal Learner Courses can complement an existing curriculum while providing opportunities to explore potential college majors and earn academic credit before graduation.
L44: A student considering a psychology degree, for example, might take an introductory course to better understand the field. Another might choose college mathematics or writing to build on subjects already studied at home. Along the way, students gain experience navigating university coursework, managing assignments and meeting college-level expectations.
L45: 
L46: Audrey Reinhardt has been able to incorporate ASU courses into her homeschool education while managing her own learning schedule.
L47: “I feel more in control of my work and pacing throughout the modules, and it has definitely taught me so much independence that I think will be irreplaceable in the future,” Reinhardt said.
L48: 
L49: She also sees value in the coursework regardless of whether a student chooses to purchase college credit. “Even if you do not end up putting it on your transcript, you still learned valuable information.”
L50: ## Is this homeschool dual enrollment?
L51: 
L52: Homeschool families exploring dual enrollment for homeschoolers can access college-level coursework through ASU Universal Learner Courses, even without an agreement between a high school and a university.
L53: Unlike traditional dual enrollment programs, which typically operate through a school or district, Universal Learner Courses allow families to enroll directly with ASU. Homeschool organizations can also participate through Accelerate ASU, the university’s nationwide dual enrollment program.
L54: ## How to include ASU courses on a homeschool transcript
L55: 
L56: Families can document completed Universal Learner Courses on their homeschool transcript, identifying the coursework as college level study through Arizona State University.
L57: 
L58: If a student chooses to purchase academic credit, the course also appears on an official ASU transcript. Families determine how coursework counts toward high school requirements according to applicable state guidelines, while ASU awards the university credit.
L59: ## Will ASU Universal Learner Courses transfer to other universities?
L60: 
L61: College credit earned through Universal Learner Courses is recorded on an official ASU transcript and may be transferable to other institutions.
L62: Each college or university determines how transferred coursework applies to its degree requirements. Families should check with prospective institutions to understand whether a course will satisfy a general education requirement, count as an elective or apply toward a particular degree program.
L63: ## Frequently asked questions
L64: 
L65: Can homeschoolers do dual enrollment? Yes. Homeschool families can take college-level coursework through 【6†ASU Universal Learner Courses】 without an agreement between a high school and a university. Families enroll directly in ULCs, the same way any other family does.
L66: Is dual enrollment worth it for homeschool students? It can be a low-risk way to try college coursework. Students pay a 【7†$25 enrollment fee】 and complete the course first. If they’re satisfied with their grade, they can pay $400 to 【8†add it to an official ASU transcript】 within one year of finishing.
L67: What is the difference between dual enrollment and concurrent enrollment? The terms are often used interchangeably, and definitions vary by state and institution. Traditional programs typically run through a school or district. 【6†Universal Learner Courses】 let families enroll directly with ASU instead.
L68: Can homeschool students take dual enrollment courses online? Yes. Universal Learner Courses are online and asynchronous, with no required live sessions. 【9†Session-based courses†courses.ulc.asu.edu】 have a set start date and weekly due dates. On-demand courses are self-paced, with a minimum of 6 weeks enrolled and one year to finish.
L69: What are the requirements to take one of the Universal Learner Courses? Students don’t apply for admission, and there are 【10†no age restrictions】 or required course prerequisites. Some courses recommend prior knowledge of certain subjects, which will be noted on the individual course webpage.
L70: Either a parent or learner can register for a course, with additional parental consent steps for learners under 18. Before starting, learners verify their identity with a live photo and an approved photo ID. Learners under 18 can use a birth certificate to begin, while 【11†proctored courses】 require a government-issued ID for the exam.
L71: Can a homeschool co-op enroll students together? Yes, if it’s a 501(c)(3). These co-ops can 【12†partner with Accelerate ASU†accelerate.asu.edu】, and they can choose to cover course costs. Students register directly, with no transcripts, applications or GPA records. Co-ops that aren’t 501(c)(3) organizations, and individual families, enroll through Universal Learner Courses.
L72: Are Universal Learner Courses accredited? Arizona State University is 【13†accredited by the Higher Learning Commission†provost.asu.edu】, and ULC credit is recorded on an official ASU transcript. Each college decides how transfer credit applies, and the 【14†Transfer Credit Guide†webapp4.asu.edu】 shows how a course may apply.
L73: 
L74: Explore ASU Universal Learner Courses
L75: Homeschool families can explore the 【9†ASU Universal Learner Course catalog†courses.ulc.asu.edu】 to find subjects, course formats and schedules that align with their student’s interests and educational goals.
L76: 
L77: 【9†Explore ASU Universal Learner Courses†courses.ulc.asu.edu】
L78: ## How much does dual enrollment cost with ASU Universal Learner Courses?
L79: 
L80: A Universal Learner Course starts with a $25 enrollment fee. The student then finishes the course and earns a grade, and nothing more is owed. A student who passes and wants the credit can pay $400 to add the course to an official ASU transcript within one year. Universal Learner Courses aren’t eligible for federal financial aid.
L81: 
L82: To enroll:
L83:   1. Choose a course and register on the 【15†how-to-enroll page】.
L84:   2. Verify the student’s identity and pay the $25 enrollment fee, which reserves the student’s spot. An email with the student’s ASURITE ID, the ASU login, arrives within 1 to 2 business days.
L85:   3. Finish the coursework and earn a grade. Nothing more is owed. A student can stop here, choose another course or retake a session-based course when it’s offered again.
L86:   4. Pay $400 only if the student passes and wants the credit. The fee adds the course to an official ASU transcript. A student has one year from finishing to decide. Once a course is on the transcript, it can’t be changed.
L87: 【9†Explore ASU Universal Learner Courses†courses.ulc.asu.edu】

L541: ## Part-Time Program Options to Help Those Who Serve Achieve Their Goals
L542: 
L543: All WGU programs are available as a military part-time option. Some programs may require full-time attendance in terms when nursing clinicals or student teaching are part of the curriculum.
L544: Part-time is only available to service members utilizing Tuition Assistance. (This option is not available to regular WGU students or to veterans using benefits under the Montgomery GI Bill). Your personal degree plan may vary based on any waivers you receive in transfer for prior academic experience. Talk to the Military Support team for details.
L545: 
L546: Email: va@wgu.edu
L547: Phone: 1-877-435-7948, ext.3127
L548: Note: Some programs are designed with integrated content and assessments that necessitate the student be enrolled full-time for at least one term. Reach out to Enrollment with any questions. GI Bill® is a registered trademark of the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs (VA). More information about education benefits offered by VA is available at the official U.S. government Web site at 【221†https://www.benefits.va.gov/gibill†www.benefits.va.gov】.

L752: ### Helpful Notes:
L753:   * Part-time tuition is set at 6–11 competency units per term for undergraduate degrees and 4–7 competency units per term for graduate degrees.
L754:   * Tuition will be adjusted by the number of competency units attempted within the term, not by time attended.
L755:   * Only tuition will be prorated. The resource fee and any program fees are still charged at the full amount for the entire term.
L756:   * Military students may be able to supplement their tuition assistance with benefits from the Montgomery GI Bill® if they are eligible.
L757:   * Federal financial aid is not available for part-time students but may be available for full-time military students.
L758:   * Students with military education benefits other than Military Tuition Assistance are not eligible for the part-time option.
L759:   * WGU reserves the right to change any of its tuition and fees. Students will be notified in advance of the new tuition rates.
L760: Tuition for the full term is due at the beginning of each term. For regular new students, payment is due on or before the 22nd of the month preceding their intended program start date. Students are responsible for payment of tuition and fees. Failure to receive payment in full by the end of the current term is grounds for administrative withdrawal.
L761: Military Tuition Assistance (TA), Post 9/11 (CH 33) and VA Voc-Rehab students may be eligible for a deferral of the tuition cost paid by their military education benefits once the appropriate form(s) has been completed, authorized, and received by WGU’s VA Department.

L120: ## Frequently asked questions about transferring to ASU
L121: ### What does it mean to be a transfer student?
L122: 
L123: A transfer student is anyone who has attended another college or university and has completed 12 or more transferable credits post-high school at the time of applying to Arizona State University. If you are completing college courses while in high school, you are considered a first-year student and not a transfer student.
L124: ### Can you transfer to Arizona State University (ASU) from a community college?
L125: 
L126: Yes, you can transfer to Arizona State University from either a community college or a university, and thousands of students do every year. ASU has strong community college partnerships and tools like 【19†MyPath2ASU®】 to help students understand how their transfer credits will apply to their degree.
L127: ### Is it hard to get into Arizona State University (ASU) as a transfer student?
L128: 
L129: No, it's not hard to transfer to Arizona State University. At ASU, we use a direct admission process, which means you can be directly admitted to almost any bachelor's degree program at ASU as long as you meet the 【78†admission requirements】 for both ASU and your major. This aligns with ASU's charter, in which we measure ourselves not by whom we exclude, but by whom we include and how they succeed.
